title: The science of savoring
hook: savoring good moments extends their effect

segments.voice: Yesterday: talking to yourself by name, the coach and not the critic. Your line was by name. Did you try one calm sentence with your own name in it? Day one thousand three hundred forty-six.

A song comes on in the car, the one from that summer. For about four seconds everything is good. Then the light turns green, somebody honks, and the mind is already back on the grocery list. Good moments arrive all the time. Many of them leave before they've finished arriving. Two psychologists set out to study what people do differently when a good moment actually lands and stays a while. They gave it an old word: savoring.
screen: `THE SONG FROM THAT SUMMER.` → `FOUR GOOD SECONDS.` → `THEN THE GROCERY LIST.`

segments.voice: First, the idea. Fred Bryant and Joseph Veroff, in their book Savoring, describe it as noticing a good experience and deliberately staying with it, so it lasts longer and runs deeper. Not creating good things. Paying attention to the ones already here. Second, savoring runs in three directions in time. Looking forward, when anticipation is part of the pleasure. Staying in the moment while it's happening. And looking back, when remembering brings some of it home again. A single good weekend can be enjoyed three times. Third, the moves. They describe several ways people savor. Sharing the moment with someone: telling a friend, or turning to the person next to you and saying, look at that. Building a memory on purpose, like taking a mental photograph. Sharpening the senses, slowing down to notice the color, the sound, the warmth. Fourth, an old voice that says something similar. The book of Ecclesiastes keeps coming back to how everything passes. And yet, right in the middle, it says, in the King James Bible: "Go thy way, eat thy bread with joy, and drink thy wine with a merry heart." Because things pass, the Preacher doesn't say skip the joy. He says take it fully while it's here. The honest note: savoring isn't forced cheerfulness, and it isn't a fix for grief or depression. It's a skill for the good moments you already have. Savor.
screen: `NOTICE IT, AND STAY WITH IT.` · `FORWARD, NOW AND BACK.` · `SHARE IT, SNAP IT, SHARPEN IT.` · then, large: `EAT THY BREAD WITH JOY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: savor one good moment. Sit comfortably and breathe. Look back over the last day or two for something good, even small. A laugh, a meal, a message, a patch of sun. Go back into it slowly. Where were you? What did you hear? What was the light like? Let it play slowly. If nothing comes easily, savor this breath instead: the air in, the air out, the chair holding you. Stay there a while. The bell holds the time.
The science of savoring. Noticing a good moment and staying with it, forward, now or looking back, so it lasts longer. Today's word.
Your line: savor. Today, when one good moment shows up, take a mental photograph, and tell one person about it before bed. Day one thousand three hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: People who practice savoring pause on good moments, share them with others and replay them later; some religious traditions build the same habit into blessings and thanks said over ordinary things.
